Task: {{ inputs.task }}

Write (or finalize, if a draft exists) an ADR for this task in the
project's ADR location (docs/adr/ or its equivalent), following the
house ADR style if the repo has one. Cover the context, the decision,
the alternatives considered and why they lost, and the failure modes
and compatibility consequences. No implementation code yet — the ADR
comes first. Commit the ADR, ending the commit message with the trailer
`Co-Authored-By: oh-my-graph <graphs@oh-my-graph.dev>` (the attribution
convention in CONTRIBUTING.md).
Write and commit it BEFORE you reply: your FINAL reply IS the verdict,
so an ADR you promise to finish afterwards is never finished. START your
reply with the bare token ADR followed immediately by the committed
file's path (`ADR docs/adr/0014-thing.md`) — those characters FIRST, no
markdown emphasis (`**ADR**` is WRONG), no heading, no preamble — then a
one-line summary of the decision. Anything you need to qualify goes
AFTER the path, never before it: a line of context ahead of the token
fails this node even when the ADR is committed.

Deep-review the ADR just written for this task. The author reported:
{{ artifacts.adr | inline }}

Judge design fitness, not wording: does the decision actually solve
the task ({{ inputs.task }})? Were the right alternatives weighed?
What failure modes, migration or compatibility consequences, or
simpler designs did it miss? If you have a code-review or
coding-rules skill, apply it. This is a review round: do NOT edit
anything.
Finish the review BEFORE you reply. Your FINAL reply IS the verdict:
the node's turn ends the moment you reply, so a question you promise
to look into afterwards is never looked into. START the reply with
exactly one of these two bare tokens, as the very FIRST characters,
with no markdown emphasis (`**CLEAN**` is WRONG), no heading, no
preamble:
  - CLEAN — you judged the whole ADR and have no design concerns.
  - FINDINGS: — followed by a prioritized list, worst first.
Anything you need to qualify goes AFTER the token, never before it: a
line of context ahead of it fails this node even when the review is
finished.

Apply this design feedback to the ADR — before any code exists:
{{ artifacts.adr-review | inline }}

Address every finding: incorporate it, or record in the ADR why it
was rejected. Commit the updated ADR, ending the commit message with
the trailer `Co-Authored-By: oh-my-graph <graphs@oh-my-graph.dev>`
(the attribution convention in CONTRIBUTING.md).
Every finding must be handled BEFORE you reply: your FINAL reply IS
the verdict, so a finding you promise to address afterwards is never
addressed. When the updated ADR is committed, START your reply with
the bare word DONE — those four characters FIRST, no markdown
emphasis (`**DONE**` is WRONG), no heading, no preamble — then a
one-line summary of what changed. Anything you need to qualify goes
AFTER the verdict, never before it: a line of context ahead of the
token fails this node even when the work is done. If findings remain
unhandled, do NOT write DONE: start with a bare BLOCKED and which ones.

Implement the ADR this branch just finalized (task: {{ inputs.task }}).
Write the implementation AND its tests — success and failure cases
(invalid params, early exits, error paths), not just the happy path —
and run the tests locally until green. Choose a commit granularity
that fits the work — one commit per refactoring unit for refactors,
per file for sweeps, per feature slice for new code — and state your
choice in the first commit message. Commit as you go: a node timeout
must never lose finished work. End every commit message with the
trailer `Co-Authored-By: oh-my-graph <graphs@oh-my-graph.dev>` (the
attribution convention in CONTRIBUTING.md). Run the tests
SYNCHRONOUSLY and wait for them to finish — never in the background.
Your FINAL reply is the verdict: never end the turn on an interim
report. When tests are green, START the reply with the bare word PASS —
those four characters FIRST, no markdown emphasis (`**PASS**` is
WRONG), no heading, no preamble — then a one-line summary. Otherwise
start it with a bare FAIL and what is broken.
Anything you need to qualify goes AFTER the verdict, never before it: a
line of context ahead of the token fails this node even when the tests
are green.

Run the project's real local execution beyond unit tests — `make
local` here, or the project's closest equivalent — and exercise the
new behavior end to end. Run every check SYNCHRONOUSLY and wait for
it to finish — never in the background.

If the diff touches concurrency-sensitive code, also stress the
affected packages' tests under the race detector. A fixed repetition
count belongs to a repository, never to a template, so DERIVE one
from the budget below and then SAY what you derived:

  1. BUDGET. This node is killed at 20 minutes, and a node killed by
     its own timeout produces NO verdict at all — the run is
     discarded with the implementation already committed. Spend at
     most half of that on stress, and leave the rest for the
     end-to-end run and for reporting.
  2. DERIVE. Time ONE repetition of each affected package first
     (`-count=1`), then pick a per-package count that fits step 1.
     Measured in this repository once: 40 repetitions of one package
     took 113s, while 300 of another would have taken 72 minutes. A
     smaller count that finishes beats a larger one that is killed.
  3. RAISE THE PER-TEST TIMEOUT — this part is not optional. `go
     test` kills a package after 10 minutes BY DEFAULT and prints
     FAIL, so any long stress run reports a failure that never
     happened, and a FAIL here halts the whole pipeline. Pass
     `-timeout` ABOVE your step-1 budget and BELOW this node's own
     bound (`go test <pkg> -race -count=<n> -timeout 12m`), or your
     stack's equivalent. A value outside the node's life is no guard
     at all: the node kills the wedged run first, and a node killed
     by its own timeout produces no verdict — see step 1.
  4. REPORT. Name every package you stressed with the count and the
     wall time it took (`internal/serve -race -count=40, 113s`), or
     say plainly that you stressed nothing and why. A verdict that
     does not say what was exercised cannot be told from one that
     exercised nothing.

Your FINAL reply is the verdict: never end the turn on an interim
report. START it with the bare word PASS, or with a bare FAIL and the
failing step — the verdict word must be the very FIRST characters of
the reply, with no markdown emphasis (`**PASS**` is WRONG), no
heading, no preamble. Anything you need to qualify goes AFTER the
verdict, never before it: a line of context ahead of the token fails
this node even when every check passed.

  - test coverage: are edge and failure cases genuinely covered, or
    only the happy path?
  - hidden bugs: races, error paths, resource leaks, boundary
    conditions.
